Intellectual property · The jurist's way · Lex Plataformae
Intellectual property

Intellectual property enters the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption as part of the infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, kept, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested, and not as a topic parallel or superior to consumer protection. Exclusivity came to organize competition and enjoyment, and the social function, read from Article 5, item XXIX, of the Federal Constitution<1><2>1</2></1>, makes it a field of reconciliation with the CDC.
Why does intellectual property enter a consumer protection regime?

In ecosystems of continuous digital consumption, intellectual property does not work only as protection of creation or as abstract economic exclusivity. It also works as part of the legal infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, kept, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested. That is why it is neither a parallel topic nor one hierarchically superior to consumer protection, because it applies inside the supply regime, as an element of governance of the object enjoyed. The relevant question is no longer who holds, in the abstract, the prerogative to modify the system, but which limits apply when this control, grounded in exclusivity, is exercised over continued enjoyment, over expectations incorporated into the relationship and over the conditions for verifying and contesting the performance.
Intellectual property only matters here insofar as it organizes power over enjoyment.<1>p. 680</1>

In ecosystems of continuous digital consumption, it does not function merely as a technique for protecting creation or as an instrument of abstract economic exclusivity. It operates, in practice, as part of the legal infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, kept, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested.<1>p. 680</1>

It is necessary to prevent intellectual property from functioning as a topic parallel, competing or hierarchically superior to consumer protection. In continuous digital services that operate Immaterial Objects of Consumption, exclusivity does not hover above the relationship as an abstract shield of ownership. It applies within the supply regime, as an element of governance of the object enjoyed.<1>p. 680</1>

It is not enough to ask who technically controls the environment or who holds, in the abstract, the prerogative to modify the system. The legally relevant question is a different one: which limits apply when this control, grounded in exclusivity, is exercised over continued enjoyment, over expectations legitimately incorporated into the relationship and over the conditions of verifiability and contestation of the performance.<1>p. 680</1>

Intellectual property should be neither reduced nor demonized, since exclusivity remains legitimate and fulfills real functions of incentive, organization and protection, but it is not an automatic authorization for opacity, opportunistic mutability or shielding against control. Where exclusivity serves to preserve creation and organize the ecosystem, it remains intelligible on its own terms. Where it operates as a technique of unilateral reconfiguration of utility, of blocking auditability, of compressing reversibility or of naturalizing opaque sanctions, it becomes part of the dogmatic problem of private governance and needs to be brought back within the limits of the social function, consumer protection and the containment of private power. It thus stops being an argument for immunity and becomes a field of reconciliation.

In this framework, intellectual property should be neither reduced nor demonized. Exclusivity remains legitimate and fulfills real functions of incentive, organization and protection. The point is only to refuse reading it as automatic authorization for opacity, for opportunistic mutability or for shielding against control.<1>p. 680</1>

When exclusivity comes to operate, in the context of supply, as a technique of unilateral reconfiguration of utility, of blocking auditability, of compressing reversibility or of naturalizing opaque sanctioning regimes, it ceases to be simple protection of an asset and becomes part of the very dogmatic problem of the private governance of the IOC.<1>p. 680</1>

What is under examination is not the exclusive right in itself, but the way it projects onto immaterial objects of consumption whose utility depends on a governed environment. Where exclusivity serves to preserve creation and organize the ecosystem, it remains intelligible on its own terms. Where it serves structural opacity, opportunistic reconfiguration, blocking of auditability and capture of enjoyment under the language of license and secrecy, it needs to be brought back within the limits imposed by the social function, by consumer protection and by the containment of private power.<1>p. 681</1>
Instead of functioning as an argument for immunity, intellectual property comes to be treated as a field of reconciliation.<1>p. 681</1>
How did intellectual property change competition in immaterial markets?

When the economic object stops being a thing delivered and circulated and becomes a continuous immaterial good, mediated by platform, account, catalog, interface and access rules, the nature of what is contested changes. What comes to matter is controlling who gets in, by which route, on what terms they stay and at what cost they can leave. The frictions that make leadership contestable in material goods, such as installed capacity, logistics and access to inputs, are partly replaced by network effects, by lock-in, which is the user's entrapment by the cost of leaving, by standardized interfaces and by the accumulation of data. Competition tends to shift toward the contest for a gatekeeping position, control over the gateways into the ecosystem, and market power becomes command over the infrastructure in which the consumer's choice becomes possible.

When the economic object ceases to be a material good, delivered and circulated as a thing, and becomes a continuous immaterial good, mediated by platform, by account, by catalog, by interface and by access rules, what economic agents compete over changes in nature. Instead of competing only on productive efficiency, on price or on the intrinsic quality of a product, what comes to matter is controlling access, that is, defining who gets in, by which route, under which conditions they stay and at what costs they can leave.<1>p. 232</1>
Installed capacity, logistics, marginal costs, access to inputs and productive dispersion function, as a rule, as brakes that make leadership relevant, but more contestable over time.<1>p. 233</1>

In immaterial goods and services mediated by platforms, the dynamic is reorganized because part of these frictions is replaced by concentration mechanisms proper to digital infrastructure. Non-rivalry and reproducibility at reduced marginal cost do not eliminate competition, but shift the terrain of the dispute to network effects, lock-in, standardization of interfaces and protocols, informational economies of scale and accumulation of data.<1>p. 233</1>

What is disputed, therefore, is the infrastructure that makes the promise consumable, and not merely the promise in the abstract. For this reason, competition in platform economies tends to take on an asymmetric design, shifting from the dispute over products to the dispute over a gatekeeping position over technical and symbolic ecosystems.<1>p. 232</1>
“Market power” exacerbates the field of participation in sales, becoming command over the very infrastructure in which the consumer's “choice” becomes possible.<1>p. 232</1>

Intellectual property enters this picture as a material component of the architecture of closure. Since reproducibility would tend to dissolve the price of immaterial goods, income depends on reintroducing scarcity by institutional decision. When this decision is coupled with license agreements, accounts, DRM, which is digital rights management, catalogs and authentication, circulation comes to be treated as infringement and enjoyment turns into authorization. From Ladislau Dowbor comes the image of the legal latifundium, the hypertrophied exclusivity that ends up withholding social utility and charging a toll on access and diffusion. The same enclosure reaches what the consumer produces in the ecosystem. A clause on user-generated content is not unlawful in itself, because it can serve hosting and circulation functions. The problem arises when the standard authorization goes beyond what is necessary and transfers to the platform ownership of the derivative works produced through the use itself.

It is here that intellectual property rights cease to appear as a peripheral legal title and come to operate as a material component of the architecture of closure. The decisive economic point is simple and direct, since, in the market for immaterial goods, reproducibility would tend to dissolve the price, so that income depends on reintroducing scarcity by institutional decision. When this decision is coupled with license agreements, accounts, DRM, catalogs and authentication mechanisms, the incentive to creation gives way to a blocking technology, which causes circulation to be treated as infringement and enjoyment to turn into authorization.<1>p. 234</1>
Acronym for Digital Right Management, “Gestão de Direitos Digitais”.<1>p. 234</1>

The metaphor of the “legal latifundium”, in Dowbor, describes a teleological dysfunction internal to the Intellectual Property regime: situations in which exclusivity, through hypertrophy of scope, duration and chains of licenses, ceases to operate predominantly as a temporary technique for stimulating future creativity and comes to function as a mechanism for the artificial retention of social utility and for charging tolls on access, recombination and diffusion of technically reproducible knowledge <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44-45)</2>.<3>p. 235</3>

In contractual terms, the presence of clauses on user-generated content (UGC) is not, in itself, unlawful, since it can fulfill operational functions of hosting, making available and circulating content in digital ecosystems.<1>p. 237</1>

Although UGC models may require licenses functionally necessary for the circulation of content in the ecosystem, the legal problem emerges when the standard authorization expands beyond what is necessary and turns into automatic appropriation of the content generated by the user, transferring to the platform ownership of creative interactions and derivative works produced in the use itself.<1>p. 237</1>

The result is an economy of cumulative permissions, in which each portion of access works as a key and the accumulation of keys turns into market power, because software, copyright-protected content, distinctive signs, design and licenses are layered over the same experience. At the extreme, Dowbor describes the tragedy of the anticommons, a concept formulated by Michael Heller and developed with Rebecca Eisenberg, in which the fragmentation of exclusivities distributes veto powers and makes recombination unlikely. For consumption, it follows that the sign of a product, in commercial discourse, may conceal an enjoyment governed by partial authorizations, which reinforces the need to make verifiable the restrictions that actually bear on the promised utility. The description is economic and does not undo the legal qualification, since Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> suffices to understand the IOC as an immaterial product, as the chapter on the object shows.
What is consolidated is an economy of cumulative permissions, in which each portion of access works as a key, and the accumulation of keys turns into market power.<1>p. 237</1>

Within the scope in view, this process shows itself through the superimposition of layers of control bearing on the same experience. One may cite, for example, software and code, copyright-protected content, distinctive signs, design and contractual license regimes, so that each layer can operate as a basis for restricting, modulating or charging for uses and circulations.<1>p. 240</1>
<1>The constitutional order and the sector framework</1>

The concept of the tragedy of the anticommons, formulated by Michael Heller and developed with Rebecca Eisenberg, describes a regime in which the fragmentation of exclusive rights distributes among multiple holders veto powers over parts, layers or components of the same resource, so that efficient use depends less on technical feasibility and more on costly legal coordination<1>p. 239</1>

For consumption, the relevant effect is that the sign of “product” may conceal an enjoyment governed by partial authorizations, reinforcing the need to make verifiable, in terms of auditability, the restrictions effectively bearing on the promised utility when governance by titles, licenses and access controls degrades the functional value of the experience.<1>p. 240</1>
What appears as a product in commercial discourse, in practice, comes to function as a bundle of fragmented, revocable and conditional authorizations.<1>p. 240</1>
Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1> already offers sufficient basis to understand the IOC as an immaterial product.<3>p. 574</3>
Why is the question not being for or against intellectual property?

Dowbor's critique is not directed against intellectual property. He recognizes the historical legitimacy of rewarding the inventor and the author and places the turning point at the moment the instrument turns into rentier charging for access. This happens, for example, when exclusivity lasts decades beyond the years in which profit is realized or when the rights almost always stay with intermediaries rather than with the creator. The question is no longer whether one is for or against intellectual property but how to calibrate it teleologically, that is, by its purpose, measuring how far exclusivity is still an incentive and at what point it becomes a structural toll. The issue is not moral but one of institutional design, and in the context of consumption it translates into criteria of loyalty, material transparency and preservation of the legitimately expected functional minimum.

The platform concentrates the mediation of access, the contract disciplines everyday use, and intellectual property supplies the grammar of blocking that turns circulation into exception and authorization into rule.<1>p. 242</1>

Dowbor does not engage in a simplistic critique of intellectual property. On the contrary, he recognizes the historical legitimacy of the incentive, understood as privileged remuneration of the inventor or author, so as to stimulate scientific and cultural advances <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 36)</2>. The turning point, however, occurs when the instrument loses social validity by turning into rentier charging for access.<3>p. 242</3>

The argument is one of political economy, since, if the realization of profit is concentrated mostly in the first years of commercial exploitation <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 43)</2>, maintaining exclusivity for decades operates as income without a proportional incentive function and imposes a massive social cost on research and creative reuse to sustain concentrated private flows.<3>p. 238</3>

The author, as the subject of intellectual creation, has little to do with this dynamic, since the rights almost always belong to intermediaries <1>Dowbor</1><2>(Dowbor, 2024, p. 44)</2>.<3>p. 238</3>

It is exactly at this point that the discussion ceases to be whether we are “against or in favor of intellectual property” and becomes “how can we teleologically calibrate intellectual property”. Because, if the real economic function of enclosure is to reinstate scarcity where technique would dissolve the price, the relevant legal problem becomes measuring how far exclusivity is still an incentive, and from what moment it becomes a structural toll. The questioning is not moral; it is a matter of institutional design, especially when the platform already dominates access and can convert any legal friction into competitive advantage.<1>p. 241</1>

Under the scope at hand, this restates the need to define criteria of loyalty, material transparency and preservation of the legitimately expected functional minimum in consumption environments mediated by platforms.<1>p. 242</1>
Why is the platform's intellectual property not a single block?

To describe what intellectual property does within supply, the central reference is Denis Borges Barbosa, for whom industrial property has always consisted of a series of techniques for controlling competition. Exclusivity is not a spontaneous quality of the immaterial good but the result of legal intervention that creates artificial scarcity, which prevents treating every power of the platform over enjoyment as if it derived from the nature of the protected asset. Hence the distinction that business discourse tends to blur. Trademarks, copyright, software, distinctive signs and interfaces do not confer the same type or the same extent of exclusivity, and the legal order does not authorize treating all technical control of the environment as if it derived from a unitary and unrestricted sovereignty.

Intellectual property does not act merely as peripheral protection of isolated assets, but as a legal technique for organizing the market and delimiting exclusivities over immaterial goods. It is in this key that Barbosa states that, in market economies, industrial property has always consisted of “a series of techniques for controlling competition”, intended to secure business investment in immaterial elements such as name, trademark, technology and institutional image <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 73)</2>.<3>p. 682</3>

Exclusivity is not a spontaneous quality of the immaterial good; it is the result of legal intervention that organizes flows of use, reproduction, circulation and exploitation <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 77-79; p. 113)</2>. This matters because it prevents naturalizing the platform's position as if every power it exercises over enjoyment derived immediately from the “nature” of the protected asset.<3>p. 682</3>

The intellectual property infrastructure that sustains the platform is not homogeneous. Trademarks, copyright, software, distinctive signs, interfaces and related institutes do not confer the same type or the same extent of exclusivity. The Brazilian legal order does not authorize treating all technical control of the environment as if it derived from a unitary and unrestricted sovereignty over the consumed experience. The very idea of intellectual property is born as a normative construction of artificial scarcity, created to make economically appropriable what, in its natural state, would circulate without equivalent barriers.<1>p. 682</1>

Each regime acts in its own layer. Trademarks delimit belonging, authenticity and the distinction between the official and what is outside the ecosystem, and the legal basis lies in Articles 122 and 123, item I, of Law 9,279/1996<1><2>3</2></1>. Copyright and related rights organize the reproduction, circulation and transformation of the expressive components of the experience, with reference to Articles 7, 28 and 29 of Law 9,610/1998<3><4>4</4></3>. Software law projects onto execution, updating, modification and stability of the environment, and Articles 7 and 8 of Law 9,609/1998<5><6>5</6></5> deal with the period of technical validity of the version marketed and the complementary technical services owed during that period. On the consumer's side, this legal concentration over signs, code and content produces semiotic vulnerability, because the consumer comes to depend on the supplier also to know what is authentic, what is official and when the experience is equivalent to what was promised.
Asymmetry ceases to be mere generic hyposufficiency and becomes structural dependence on meaning and verifiability.<1>p. 687</1>

Trademarks delimit belonging, authenticity and the distinction between the official and what is outside the ecosystem. Copyright and related rights organize the possibility of reproduction, circulation and transformation of the expressive components of the experience. Software law, in turn, projects directly onto execution, updating, modification and stability of the environment.<1>p. 683</1>

“Art. 122. Visually perceptible distinctive signs are eligible for registration as a trademark [...]. Art. 123. [...] the following is considered: I - product or service trademark: one used to distinguish a product or service from another identical, similar or related one, of different origin;” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]c)</2>.<3>p. 683</3>

“Art. 7 Protected intellectual works are creations of the mind, expressed by any means or fixed on any medium, tangible or intangible, known or to be invented in the future, such as:” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2021])</2>.<3>p. 683</3>

“Art. 7 The license agreement for use of a computer program, the corresponding tax document, the physical media of the program or the respective packaging shall state, in a form easily legible by the user, the period of technical validity of the version marketed.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [1998])</2>.<3>p. 683</3>

“Art. 8 Whoever markets a computer program [...] is obliged, in the national territory, during the period of technical validity of the respective version, to ensure to the respective users the provision of complementary technical services relating to the proper functioning of the program, considering its specifications.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [1998])</2>.<3>p. 683</3>

The consumer does not depend on the supplier only to access the object technically; they also depend on the supplier to understand what is authentic, what is official, what counts as valid belonging, what may circulate, what may be kept and under what conditions the experience will be deemed equivalent to what was promised. The legal concentration over signs, code, content and channels of circulation produces semiotic vulnerability not only through an information deficit, but because the platform controls the very means by which the offer is understood, equivalence is perceived, loss is recognized and proof is produced.<1>p. 687</1>
What does software protection authorize and what does it not authorize?

Software is the most sensitive point, because the platform often acts as if the protection of the technological infrastructure gave it practical sovereignty over the whole consumed experience. As Barbosa shows, the protection of computer programs in Brazilian law is predominantly a matter of copyright and bears on the expression of useful solutions, that is, on the code and certain non-literal manifestations, without being organized as a general patent over functionality, method of operation or user experience. Even when the program takes part in a new and inventive technical effect, the patent bears on a delimited technical solution, and not on the result, and the algorithm considered in the abstract remains free. Barbosa also notes that not all software is patentable in Brazil and that the unconditional prohibition of patents for business methods remains. This is enough to block the rhetoric that depending on protected code would authorize absolute control over mutability, auditability, functional equivalence and contestation of enjoyment.

In the case of software, this tension takes on an even more precise contour. The platform often acts as if the legal protection of the technological infrastructure conferred on it practical sovereignty over the whole consumed experience, when the Brazilian regime does not deliver that.<1>p. 698</1>

In Brazilian law, the protection of computer programs is not organized as a general patent over functionality, method of operation or user experience. Its protection is predominantly copyright-based, and even when a program takes part in obtaining a new and inventive technical effect, the patent does not project onto the software as such, nor onto the abstract logic underlying the consumed experience. Patent protection bears on a delimited technical solution, not on the result in the abstract nor on all the functionality perceived by the user <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1128; p. 1116)</2>.<3>p. 684</3>

Barbosa states precisely that software is primarily protected by a copyright-type regime, which bears on the expression of useful solutions, that is, on the code and certain non-literal manifestations, but does not reach solutions of technical effect as such.<1>p. 685</1>

Barbosa is categorical in stating that, in Brazilian law, not all software will be eligible for patent protection, but only some inventions relating to computer programs, which is why, with even more force, the unconditional prohibition on granting patents for business methods subsists among us <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1136)</2>.<3>p. 685-686</3>

Even in the exceptional cases in which the program takes part in a patentable technical solution, the algorithm considered in the abstract remains free, and the program as such does not become the object of a patent in a broad sense <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1123-1124)</2>. This is enough to block a very common rhetoric on platforms: that the mere fact that the environment depends on protected code would authorize, without remainder, absolute control over mutability, auditability, functional equivalence and contestation of enjoyment.<3>p. 685</3>

Containment does not lead to the opposite extreme. Software is not legally neutral, because running it and making it work already involves the exercise of an intellectual right, and license, control of execution and discipline of updates are recognized instruments for organizing this power. Barbosa observes, however, that the primary source of a program's value lies in its behavior, and not in the text, and that copyright protection does not extend to the method of operation. Once in commerce, certain subsequent effects escape the reach of exclusivity, and insisting on controlling them as a natural extension of the title may constitute abuse of rights, just as the use of intellectual property rights to dominate markets or limit access may constitute an infringement of the economic order. On the basis of this regime, it is incompatible with the Constitution to convert technical control of the infrastructure into total power over the consumed experience, and the social function operates as a brake against this overreach.
The value of the program is not to be confused with the text itself, and text and behavior are not the same thing legally.<1>p. 687</1>

[...] the centrality of software in the platform's infrastructure does not authorize presenting it as a source of unlimited legal power over everything the consumer experiences in the ecosystem. None of this means, on the other hand, that software is legally neutral or marginal. On the contrary. Its protection regime participates directly in control over the use, execution, updating, maintenance and exploitation of the program. Running the software, using it and making it work already involves the exercise of an intellectual right, and not mere use of a physical medium, which helps explain why the computing infrastructure participates immediately in organizing the enjoyment of the IOC <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2015; p. 1959)</2>.<3>p. 686</3>

Of course the protection of software explains an important part of the platform's technical power. License, control of execution and discipline of updates are legally recognized instruments for organizing this power.<1>p. 699</1>

Barbosa underlines exactly this point when observing that one of the greatest discussions in the field of intellectual property applied to software stems from the fact that the primary source of a program's value lies not in the text itself, but in its behavior, it being possible for distinct codes to lead to identical functional results <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1899)</2>.<3>p. 687</3>

Although he recognizes that copyright protection is not limited to the literal expression of the instructions, and may also reach the way the elements composing the software are organized, Barbosa warns that, “insofar as the internal form is directly related to functionality, it will not be protected by Copyright”, since the latter “does not protect the structure in itself”; in other words, “the authorial protection of the program does not extend to the method of operation” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1890)</2>.<3>p. 687</3>

Once in commerce, certain subsequent effects escape the reach of exclusivity, and insisting on controlling them as if everything were still a natural extension of the title may constitute abuse of rights <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010b, p. 1145; p. 1139)</2>. This means that control of the code, execution and updating does not authorize, without more, blocking verifiability, neutralizing the assessment of functional loss or reducing enjoyment to a disposable permission administered ad nutum.<3>p. 698-699</3>

In Brazilian law, the use of intellectual property rights to dominate the market or limit access may constitute an infringement of the economic order, in light of the constitutional protection of freedom of competition <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2025)</2>.<3>p. 699</3>

Since the protection of programs in Brazil is not structured under a broad patent logic over function, method or result, but under a special, predominantly authorial regime, it is incompatible with the Constitution to convert technical control of the infrastructure into total power over the consumed experience.<1>p. 706</1>
The social function operates, here, as a brake against this overreach.<1>p. 707</1>
Why do trademarks and industrial design matter on the consumer's side?

The layer of signs is the other side of the argument. The trademark is one of the clearest examples of the juridification of the semiotic layer of the market, because protection bears on the sign's aptitude to identify and distinguish products or services. José Carlos Tinoco Soares requires a trademark to be distinctive, special and unmistakable, and Douglas Gabriel Domingues highlights its advertising function and the symbolic universes of prestige and status associated with it. If the legal order recognizes that signs produce real economic, competitive and legal effects, there is no honest basis to deny that the same signs, when they govern enjoyment, also structure expectation, belonging, reputation and perceived functional value. When the layer of signs protects the supplier's origin and clientele, its relevance is promptly recognized, and when it structures the way the consumer perceives authenticity, equivalence and loss, traditional legal discourse tends to retreat. There is an asymmetry of legal visibility here.

The trademark offers, among the institutes of intellectual property, one of the clearest examples of the juridification of the semiotic layer of the market. Its protection does not bear only on a word, figure or formally registrable medium, but on the sign's aptitude to present, mark, identify and distinguish products or services in economic traffic.<1>p. 687-688</1>

Not by chance, classical doctrine describes it precisely as the sign by which the product or service becomes known and distinguished in the market, requiring, for the fulfillment of this purpose, that it be distinctive, special and unmistakable <1>Soares</1><2>(Soares, 2000, p. 16; p. 109)</2>.<3>p. 688</3>

The very evolution of trademark doctrine reveals that the economic centrality of the trademark depends less on the physical medium than on its capacity to condense identity, fix perception and guide the consumer's choice, including through its advertising function and the constitution of symbolic universes associated with the product, the prestige and the social status it represents <1>Domingues</1><2>(Domingues, 1984, p. 70-71; p. 89)</2>.<3>p. 689</3>

If the legal order recognizes that signs produce real economic, competitive and legal effects, there is no honest basis to deny that these same signs, when they come to govern enjoyment in continuous digital ecosystems, also structure expectation, belonging, reputation, perceived functional value and consumer vulnerability.<1>p. 689</1>

It is not, therefore, a matter of discovering a new type of phenomenon, but of correcting an asymmetry of legal visibility. When the sign layer organizes origin, differentiation and attraction of clientele in favor of the supplier, its relevance is promptly recognized. When this same layer comes to structure the criteria by which the consumer perceives authenticity, officialness, equivalence and relevant loss within the platform, the tendency of traditional legal discourse is to retreat before its immaterial dimension. What this thesis proposes is precisely to refuse this selective blindness.<1>p. 689-690</1>

Industrial design gives additional evidence. Article 95 of Law 9,279/1996<1><2>6</2></1> protects the ornamental plastic form that provides a new and original visual result in the external configuration of the object, and with this the law recognizes the ornamental form as an element of attraction and differentiation, beyond technical function. Barbosa speaks of the seductive power of aesthetic configuration and gives the example of the plate decorated with a protected figure, which may be the object of exclusivity, while the same plate without the design remains free, so that the boundary of protection lies in the aesthetic investment, and not in utility. It follows that the visuals of interfaces, the aesthetic composition of skins, which are the appearances bought for characters, the graphic effects and the visually coded signs of rarity take part in the economy of belonging and perceived value. The difference between the decorated corporeal object and the continuously enjoyed immaterial object only shifts the medium.
Intellectual property law, therefore, protects not only what distinguishes by reference to a sign; it also protects what seduces by aesthetic shaping.<1>p. 691</1>

“Art. 95. Industrial design is considered to be the ornamental plastic form of an object or the ornamental set of lines and colors that may be applied to a product, providing a new and original visual result in its external configuration and that may serve as a type of industrial manufacture.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2024]c)</2>.<3>p. 691</3>

The dogmatically relevant point here is that the law does not limit itself to protecting technical function, material utility or business origin. It recognizes, in its own key, the legal relevance of ornamental form as an element of market insertion, attraction and differentiation of the good.<1>p. 691</1>

The protection of industrial design starts precisely from the premise that the aesthetic configuration of the product can add seductive power and greater commercial value to it, directly bending the public's choice.<1>p. 691</1>

The example is eloquent: a plate decorated with a protected figure may be the object of exclusivity, while the same plate, identical in size, material and functionality, but lacking that design, remains free for reproduction by third parties <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 50)</2>. The boundary of protection does not lie, therefore, in the materiality of the good nor in its practical function, but in the aesthetic investment incorporated into its external configuration.<3>p. 691</3>

In continuous consumption environments, the visuals of interfaces, the aesthetic composition of skins, distinctive finishes, graphic effects, visually coded signs of rarity and the iconographic coherence of the universe offered to the user are not neutral elements or external to enjoyment. They take part in the very economy of belonging, attractiveness and perceived value, functioning as components of the semiotic governance of the IOC. The difference between the decorated corporeal object and the continuously enjoyed immaterial object does not erase this structural fact; it only shifts its medium.<1>p. 693-694</1>

The analogy has an express limit. It does not equate distinct legal regimes nor convert skins, interfaces or visual arrangements into industrial designs, and the proposed step does not dissolve trademark law into consumer law. The distinctive and ornamental layer may take on consumer law relevance when it operates as a technique of inducement, opacity, identity capture or relevant functional degradation. The Constitution, in turn, links the protection of industrial creations and signs to the social interest and to development and subjects the economic order to the social function of property and to consumer protection, so that exclusivity is legitimate, but not metaphysically sovereign.
The analogy, here, does not seek to equate distinct legal regimes nor to automatically convert skins, interfaces or digital visual arrangements into industrial designs.<1>p. 693</1>
The step proposed by this thesis does not consist in dissolving trademark law into consumer law, nor in denying the legitimacy of distinctive protection in favor of the holder.<1>p. 690</1>

If so, the distinctive layer that forms part of the enjoyment of IOCs cannot be treated as mere off-the-books decoration of the experience. It forms part of the very semiotic governance of supply and, for that reason, may take on consumer law relevance when it operates as a technique of inducement, opacity, identity capture or relevant functional degradation.<1>p. 690</1>

On the one hand, intellectual property is a legitimate foundation for the organization of the market and competitive predictability. The right to property is constitutionally guaranteed, and the protection of industrial creations, trademarks and other distinctive signs is born, in the constitutional text, linked to the social interest and to the technological and economic development of the country. On the other, the same constitutional order places this exclusivity back within material limits, by subjecting the economic order to the social function of property and to consumer protection. In other words, exclusivity is legitimate, but it is not metaphysically sovereign.<1>p. 694</1>
What does the intellectual property clause in a game's terms reveal?

The point appears clearly in clause 3.2 of the Terms of Service of Riot Games, the company that operates League of Legends. In it the company and its licensors reserve all rights over the services and over the data and content generated or made available in them, including user accounts, code, characters, chat logs, which are the records of conversations, recordings, virtual goods, in-game currency, audiovisual effects, methods of operation and gameplay. The same clause allows some personal and non-commercial uses, such as fan art, which is art made by fans, and prohibits unlicensed uses of trademarks, content and services.

I can do things with Riot's intellectual property (We reserve all rights to our IP, but we allow some personal and non-commercial uses, such as fan art.) We (and our licensors) own and reserve all rights, title and interests in the Riot Services, as well as in all data and content published, generated, provided or otherwise made available on or through the Riot Services, including user accounts, computer code, titles, objects, artifacts, characters, character names, chat logs, game recordings and broadcasts, locations, location names, stories, dialogue, catchphrases, art, graphics, structural or landscape designs, animations, sounds, musical compositions and recordings, virtual goods, in-game currency, audiovisual effects, image and graphic likeness of characters, methods of operation and gameplay (collectively, “Game Content”).<1>p. 684</1>

You also agree that, unless we grant you a license, in a signed written contract, you may never use any of our trademarks, service marks, trade names, logos, domain names, brand slogans or trade dress. Any reproduction, redistribution or modification of the Riot Services, or use of the Riot Services not in accordance with this Agreement, is expressly prohibited and may result in severe civil and/or criminal penalties.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 684</3>

The clause reads as a description of the ecosystem. By reserving all this, the company does not merely protect assets, and it describes, in contractual terms, an environment in which intellectual property organizes the experience, authenticity and circulation of the content enjoyed, so that control over signs, gameplay and visuals is part of the infrastructure through which the environment is governed. In League of Legends, distinctiveness reaches internal signs of officialness, rarity, authenticity, prestige and valid belonging. On the competition level, the unilateral alteration of an item's appearance, effects or place in the internal economy operates as an exercise of competitive power, because it redefines after the purchase the meaning and utility of the good, without the consumer having an equivalent route to restoration outside the ecosystem.

The “rare” cosmetic item is not rare by technical nature, since its reproduction is trivial, but because the platform administers scarcity, prestige and circulation as internal variables of its own market, converting technical abundance into economic scarcity.<1>p. 233-234</1>

By reserving for itself and its licensors all rights, title and interests in the services, game content, accounts, code, characters, logs, recordings, virtual goods, in-game currency, audiovisual effects, methods of operation and gameplay, and by prohibiting unlicensed uses of trademarks, content and services, Riot does not merely protect assets. It describes, in contractual terms, an ecosystem in which IP works as the matrix for organizing the experience, authenticity and circulation of the content enjoyed.<1>p. 684</1>

The clause is revealing because it shows, bluntly, that control over signs, narratives, gameplay, visuals and content is not peripheral to supply. It is part of the very infrastructure through which the environment is governed. This becomes even more sensitive in the case of software.<1>p. 684</1>

Distinctiveness does not operate only at the level of the Riot corporate trademark or the trademark of the game itself, but also in the administration of internal signs of officialness, rarity, authenticity, prestige, lawfulness of circulation, community recognition and valid belonging.<1>p. 690</1>

The unilateral alteration of appearance, effects or the item's insertion into the internal economy, as in the scenario described, operates as an exercise of competitive power because it redefines ex post the meaning and utility of the good within the proprietary language, without the consumer having an equivalent route to restoration outside the ecosystem.<1>p. 234</1>

From the clause the examination passes directly to software, where the point becomes even more sensitive. Since the authorial protection of the program does not extend to the method of operation nor make the holder of the code the absolute holder of the functional result experienced by the user, control over execution, updating and modulation cannot be expanded, by contract or rhetoric, to the point of erasing the consumer law density of continuously supplied enjoyment. Applied to the case, the construction produces a reading guide, and not a conclusion about the clause or about the company. The declared ownership remains, in principle, legitimate, and the analysis shifts from the abstract level of the title's existence to the concrete level of its exercise. When the platform invokes exclusivity, system integrity or software protection to justify blocks, reconfigurations, suppressions or deletions, it is on this level that minimum verifiability, the requirement of reasons, assessment of functional loss, the possibility of contestation and, where appropriate, restoration of the relevant effects apply.

The authorial protection of software does not extend to the method of operation in itself, nor does it turn the holder of the code into the absolute holder of the functional result experienced by the user <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1890; p. 1899)</2>. This distinction is central, because it prevents control over execution, updating and modulation of the program from being expanded, by contract or rhetoric, to the point of erasing the consumer law density of continuously supplied enjoyment.<3>p. 687</3>

The very idea of intellectual property coexists with internal and external limitations that make it absurd to treat it as unrestricted authorization for use and government of the ecosystem <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 3; p. 13])</2>. This matters because it shifts the analysis from the abstract level of the title's existence to the concrete level of its exercise over the consumed experience.<3>p. 696-697</3>

When the platform invokes exclusivity, system integrity, operational necessity or software protection to justify blocks, reconfigurations, suppressions or deletions, the legal problem does not end with the abstract validity of the prerogative invoked. It shifts to the control of the concrete way this power is exercised over governed enjoyment. It is on this level that minimum verifiability, the requirement of reasons, assessment of functional loss, the possibility of contestation and, where appropriate, restoration of the relevant effects must apply.<1>p. 702</1>
Where, after all, is the tension between exclusivity and consumer protection?

The tension arises from the undue leap between having an intellectual property right and assuming, from it, total power to alter conditions of use, impose private sanctions, suppress accumulated trajectories and block the reconstruction of what was done, and this collision is not theoretical but a practical conflict of governance over continued enjoyment. The excess begins in the vocabulary. José de Oliveira Ascensão points out that qualifying intellectual rights under the sign of property favors the tendential elimination of their limits and carries an ideological charge. He also recalls that the legal rule artificially makes scarce goods that are not scarce, hence the predominantly negative content of intellectual rights, which confer a power to exclude third parties, and not positive sovereignty over every experience around the good. The consequence is that revocable license, unilateral mutability, banning or deletion of a trajectory cannot be treated as self-justified effects of mere ownership.
Intellectual exclusivity is a delimited normative construction, not metaphysical sovereignty over all projections of the ecosystem.<1>p. 695</1>

The problem does not lie in the abstract existence of exclusivity, but in the undue leap between having an IP right and assuming, from it, total power to alter conditions of use, reconfigure the experience, impose private sanctions, suppress accumulated trajectories and block the institutional reconstruction of what was done.<1>p. 695</1>
The collision, here, is not theoretical. It is a practical conflict of private governance over continuously supplied enjoyment.<1>p. 695</1>

Ascensão is right to point out that qualifying intellectual rights under the sign of property favors the tendential elimination of their limits and that this operation has a clearly ideological, not descriptive, charge <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 3; p. 5])</2>. Consequently, revocable license, unilateral mutability, banning or deletion of a trajectory cannot be treated as self-justified effects of mere IP ownership.<3>p. 695-696</3>

Ascensão is direct in stating that the legal rule “artificially makes scarce goods that are not scarce” and that “this is the technique of the exclusive” <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 12])</2>. For that very reason, the content of the intellectual right is predominantly negative: it does not confer on the holder unlimited positive power over the object, but a faculty of exclusion vis-à-vis third parties.<3>p. 696</3>

Barbosa reaches the same place by the Brazilian route. Each exclusive right exists within the limits and for the functions constitutionally assigned to it, and the principle remains that of freedom. The very exercise of copyright may be abusive, the patent is an instrumental monopoly that admits containment such as the compulsory license, and exhaustion prevents endless control over the good already placed in commerce. Barbosa also recalls that the TRIPS Agreement, the expression of the international intellectual property regime, does not enshrine an absolutist paradigm. This defeats the use of intellectual property as a terminal argument, which would close the discussion before it began, and places the meeting between it and the CDC in the control of the way exclusivity is used in the consumer relationship.

The same conclusion appears, in a Brazilian key, in the reading of Denis Borges Barbosa. Exclusivity in intellectual property exists within the limits and for the functions constitutionally assigned to it, not as a general authorization to govern without restraint all enjoyment of the environment. The principle remains that of freedom; exclusivity is a functionally delimited exception <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84; p. 537; p. 547)</2>.<3>p. 697</3>

The very exercise of copyright may be abusive, and the patent, as an instrumental monopoly, coexists with containment mechanisms and with the logic of exhaustion, which prevents endless control over all subsequent forms of enjoyment of the good already placed in commerce <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 110; p. 639; p. 671)</2>.<3>p. 697</3>

The patent, as an “instrumental monopoly”, does not subsist as sovereign discretion, admitting means of containment such as compulsory licensing and price control <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 639)</2>.<3>p. 697</3>

The departure from absolutism is explicit in the international regime, since the TRIPS Agreement does not enshrine an absolutist paradigm, being based on a balance between promoting innovation and diffusing technology <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2>.<3>p. 698</3>

Not even the international regime enshrines a totalizing paradigm; on the contrary, it works with a balance between incentive and diffusion, between protection and limits <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75-76; p. 662)</2>. This defeats the claim to use IP as a terminal argument that would close, before it even began, the discussion about good faith, restoration, verifiability and control of private power.<3>p. 698</3>

Exclusivity does not operate as a safe-conduct to turn technical infrastructure into an unrestricted instrument for the material suppression of the contract's utility or for neutralizing control over its effects <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 2025; p. 2030; p. 2026)</2>. This is the exact point at which IP and CDC meet: not in the denial of exclusivity, but in the control of the way it is used in the consumer relationship.<3>p. 699</3>
Does calling the relationship a license set the CDC aside?

The language of the revocable license does not save the platform either, as Claudia Lima Marques shows. In consumer relationships, the binding force of the text is not measured only by formal acceptance, but by its compatibility with good faith and balance, because the will expressed in the contract is no longer, for the author, an isolated decisive factor. Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1> works as a general clause prohibiting iniquitous obligations or obligations incompatible with equity. Nor is the name given to the transaction the decisive factor in characterizing the consumer contract, so that license, exclusivity or technological secrecy do not take the relationship out of the consumer law regime when there is continued supply under exploitable vulnerability. Bruno Miragem adds that, when the utility of the product depends on software, the captivity created by continuous updates broadens the relevance of the duty to inform in advance of the terms of these changes, and that restrictions of use and relevant alterations not clarified in the offer may give rise to an information defect, abusiveness and frustration of legitimate expectations.
Calling it a license does not erase the structure of continued supply nor eliminate the material scrutiny of the CDC.<1>p. 700</1>

In this scenario, the language of the revocable license does not save the platform either. In consumer relationships, the binding force of the contractual text is not measured only by formal acceptance, but by its compatibility with good faith and balance. The will expressed in a contract is no longer an isolated decisive factor, and clauses that seek to turn continued enjoyment into a revocable favor, emptying its legal density, are not self-justified merely because they were predisposed in an adhesion contract <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1004; p. 1080-1081)</2>.<3>p. 700</3>

Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<1><2>7</2></1> works as a general clause prohibiting provisions that establish iniquitous obligations or obligations incompatible with equity <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1080-1081)</4>.<5>p. 700</5>

To characterize the consumer contract, the decisive factor is not the existence of a special law or the name given to the transaction, but the presence of a consumer in a materially protectable position <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 612)</2>.<3>p. 701</3>

License, exclusivity or technological secrecy do not remove the relationship from the consumer law regime when there is continued supply under exploitable vulnerability <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 471; p. 481; p. 612)</2>.<3>p. 701</3>

When the utility of the product depends on software, failures in this supply can remove all its value, and the captivity created by continuous updates further broadens the relevance of the duty to inform in advance of the terms of these mutations. Restrictions of use and relevant alterations need to be clarified in the offer; otherwise, they may give rise to an information defect, abusiveness and frustration of legitimate expectations <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 86; p. 79])</2>. The name of the contractual technique does not change the density of the harm.<3>p. 701</3>

There is also an inversion internal to the field itself. Article 27 of Law 9,610/1998<1><2>8</2></1> declares the author's moral rights inalienable and unwaivable, and the provision does not enter to make the consumer's experience authorial nor to transplant the authorial moral logic to the IOC. Its role is more restrained. It shows that the language of intellectual property is not reduced to absolute patrimonial disposability and already knows, from within, limits to the complete dissolution of immaterial bonds. This reinforces that license, adhesion and technical control are not enough, by themselves, to erase the legal density of the memory and continuity of enjoyment built in the ecosystem.

The Brazilian copyright regime is not exhausted in the patrimonial facet of exploitation. It also maintains a core of moral rights expressly qualified as inalienable and unwaivable. This provision does not enter here to make the consumer's experience authorial nor to transplant, without mediation, the authorial moral logic to the field of the IOC. Its role is more restrained and more elegant: to show that the very language of IP is not reduced to absolute patrimonial disposability and already knows, from within, limits to the complete dissolution of relevant immaterial bonds. This reinforces the argument that license, adhesion and technical control are not enough, by themselves, to erase all legal density of the memory, traceability and continuity of enjoyment built in the governed ecosystem.<1>p. 702</1>
“Art. 27. The author's moral rights are inalienable and unwaivable.” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2021])</2>.<3>p. 702</3>
What does Article 5, item XXIX, of the Constitution require of exclusivity?

Containment does not derive only from good faith, exhaustion, the prohibition of abuse or the critique of proprietary absolutism, and it derives from the Constitution itself. Article 5, item XXIX, of the Federal Constitution<1><2>1</2></1> ensures a temporary privilege for industrial inventions and protects industrial creations, trademarks, company names and other distinctive signs, in view of the social interest and the technological and economic development of the country. The reading of the item, supported by an earlier study by Andrade on industrial property in the Constitution, has three steps. In the first, the provision selects objects and imposes a purpose on them, and industrial creations is read in a broad material key, so that there is no narrow clause aimed only at the patent, but a frame over the patrimonial-industrial set of creations and signs. In the second, the phrase in view of is purposive, and social interest designates the synthesis of the general needs of the community, while development is not to be confused with quantitative growth or rent extraction.

This containment does not derive only from objective good faith, exhaustion, the prohibition of abuse or the doctrinal critique of proprietary absolutism. It derives from the Constitution itself. In dealing with industrial property, Article 5, XXIX does not grant a self-justified patrimonial prerogative, nor does it protect exclusivity as an end in itself.<1>p. 702</1>

“Art. 5. [...] XXIX - the law shall ensure to the authors of industrial inventions a temporary privilege for their use, as well as protection for industrial creations, the ownership of trademarks, company names and other distinctive signs, in view of the social interest and the technological and economic development of the country [...].” <1>Brasil</1><2>(Brasil, [2025]a)</2>.<3>p. 694</3>
The provision does not merely mention industrial property among constitutionally recognized rights. It selects its objects and imposes a purpose on them.<1>p. 703</1>

We are not, therefore, faced with a narrow clause aimed only at the patent, but with a constitutional frame bearing on the patrimonial-industrial set of creations and signs protected in the competitive environment <1>al.</1><2>(Andrade, 2021, p. 61-66)</2>.<3>p. 704</3>

The phrase “in view of” performs an unequivocal purposive function: legal protection is only justified while oriented to the social interest and to the technological and economic development of the country. Social interest, here, is not reduced to the abstract convenience of the market nor to the private interest of the holder maximized to the limit. It designates the synthesis of the general needs of the Brazilian community, assessable according to the historical, economic and social context in which protection is applied. Likewise, development is not to be confused with mere quantitative growth or rent extraction.<1>p. 704</1>

The third step is scope. The item operates as a norm of shaping and limitation addressed to the legislator, the interpreter and the one who applies the law, because, by saying that the law shall ensure, the Constitution conditions the material validity of the protective norms and of their application on the purposes it states, and the Industrial Property Law is only constitutionally acceptable within this frame. Functionalization, therefore, is internal to the regime. Barbosa describes intellectual property as more conditioned and less full than other forms of property, and Ascensão treats the limits of the exclusive right as a normal part of its shaping, a negation of the negation that keeps the channels of information, competition and culture open. On platforms, this means that exclusivity cannot serve as a shield against the control of abusiveness when its exercise makes decisions opaque, imposes unilateral mutations, makes minimum auditing unfeasible or destroys, without restoration, the functional core of the promised enjoyment.
The power exists, but it exists functionalized.<1>p. 705</1>

Article 5, XXIX operates as a constitutional norm of shaping and limitation, addressed both to the infraconstitutional legislator and to the interpreter and the one who applies the law. By saying that “the law shall ensure”, the Constitution not only authorizes the enactment of protective norms; it conditions the very material validity of these norms and of their application on the purposes it itself states. The Industrial Property Law and any other patrimonial discipline relating to industrial creations are constitutionally acceptable only insofar as they are compatible with this purposive frame. Outside it, what arises is not a mere regulatory inconvenience, but a constitutionally qualified tension. On IOC platforms, this means that exclusivity cannot be mobilized as a shield against the control of abusiveness when its concrete exercise serves to make decisions opaque, impose unilateral mutations of the experience, make minimum auditing unfeasible or destroy, without restoration, the functional core of the promised enjoyment.<1>p. 704</1>

The Constitution does ensure industrial property, but it ensures it under a condition. And a constitutional condition is not rhetorical ornament; it is a criterion of validity, interpretation and containment of private power <1>al.</1><2>(Andrade, 2021, p. 109-110)</2>. This conditioning does not act as an external, accidental or exceptional brake. Functionalization is internal to the IP regime itself. It is a form of property even more conditioned, even more socially responsible and less full than other proprietary forms, precisely because the exclusive right exists to balance private interests of exploitation and public interests of access, progress and socially useful circulation of the immaterial <3>Barbosa</3><4>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</4>.<5>p. 704-705</5>

The limits of the exclusive right are neither external anomalies nor occasional concessions to the vulnerable party. They are a normal part of its shaping, a true “negation of the negation”, indispensable for keeping the channels of information, competition, culture and social communication open <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 11; p. 13; p. 14])</2>.<3>p. 706</3>
How does the social function translate into duties on the platform?

When supply is continued and enjoyment depends on private infrastructure, the exercise of intellectual property ceases to be only dominion over an asset and becomes a power to organize consumption trajectories, expectations and reputational positions. The constitutional economic order, by subjecting property to the social function and linking it with consumer protection, prevents dissociating exclusivity from the functional integrity of supply. Miragem argues that consumer vulnerability justifies norms limiting private power, and on platforms this translates into duties of clarity, verifiability and preservation of functional utility. It thus becomes unlawful to use technical exclusivity to disguise planned obsolescence, lower the quality of performance without justification or block the auditability of contractual performance. The social function does not replace the dogmatics of the CDC, and reinforces it constitutionally. Nor is it necessary to resort to a strong idea of consumer property to demand minimum stability, which derives from the consumer relationship itself, and what is protected is the functional and, where appropriate, biographical and symbolic integrity of the promised enjoyment.

When supply is continued and enjoyment depends on private infrastructure, the exercise of property and IP ceases to be only dominion over an asset and becomes, concretely, a power to organize consumption trajectories, expectations, reputational positions and possibilities of participation in the ecosystem. The constitutional economic order already makes this visible by subjecting property to the social function and by linking this functionalization with consumer protection. In IOCs, this linkage means that the exercise of exclusivity cannot be dissociated from the functional integrity of supply and from the protection of the vulnerable party against the arbitrariness of whoever holds technical control of the environment.<1>p. 707</1>

Consumer vulnerability justifies norms limiting private power precisely to prevent factual and technical superiority from turning into material suppression of rights. On IOC platforms, this translates into duties of clarity, verifiability and preservation of functional utility, making it unlawful to use technical exclusivity to disguise planned obsolescence, lower the quality of performance without justification or block the auditability of contractual performance <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274)</2>. The social function, here, does not replace the dogmatics of the CDC. It reinforces it constitutionally.<3>p. 707</3>

Nor is it necessary to resort to a strong idea of consumer property over the digital good to demand minimum stability. This stability derives from the very structure of the consumer relationship and from the protection of legitimate expectations in continued contracts, especially when the platform controls the conditions of intelligibility of the object and concentrates the proof of what was altered. What is protected, then, is not a mirrored dominion of the consumer over the asset, but the functional and, where appropriate, biographical and symbolic integrity of the promised enjoyment.<1>p. 708</1>

In this framework, open auditability and functional value equivalence appear as concretizations compatible with the social function, and not as attacks on the core of exclusivity. Open auditability works as a functional unfolding of this constitutional limit, while remaining an internal unfolding of the duty to inform, and it requires only that relevant alterations and sanctions with material impact be justifiable in an intelligible and verifiable way, without unrestricted opening of code. On platforms, the social function translates into four workable criteria. They are the duty of verifiable justification for relevant alterations, the minimum preservation of records and trails for institutional control, restoration by functional equivalence when there is substantial loss of the core of enjoyment and the prohibition on using technical dependence as a mechanism of private exclusion without a minimum standard of control.

It is at this point that the constructed operators appear as concretizations compatible with the social function, and not as undue attacks on the core of exclusivity. Open auditability works as a functional unfolding of this constitutional limit. It does not require unrestricted opening of code, nor a broad exposure of the protected asset. It requires only that relevant alterations and sanctions with material impact be justifiable in a technically intelligible and institutionally verifiable way, compatible with control by protection bodies and by the Judiciary.<1>p. 708</1>

On IOC platforms, this limit translates into workable criteria: a duty of verifiable justification for relevant alterations, minimum preservation of records and trails for institutional control, a requirement of restoration by functional equivalence when there is substantial loss of the core of enjoyment and a prohibition on using technical dependence as a mechanism of private exclusion without a minimum standard of control.<1>p. 710</1>
What happens when the service is shut down?

The treatment of the shutdown of the service does not rest on a cited author nor on a specific provision, and it develops from the social function of property and of intellectual property within the constitutional framework set out in this chapter. In cases of termination of activities, discontinuation of services or permanent shutdown of servers, the formal precariousness of use licenses can no longer be read as automatic authorization for the complete sacrifice of immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into the consumer's trajectory. Histories, libraries, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be treated as residues without density just because they are housed in someone else's infrastructure. Exclusivity is not enough to legitimize the deletion of these collections under the pretext of business freedom, economic convenience or strategic reorientation.

This limit takes on a particularly sharp contour in cases of termination of activities, discontinuation of services or permanent shutdown of servers. As relevant portions of contemporary life migrate to private digital ecosystems, the formal precariousness of use licenses can no longer be read as automatic authorization for the complete sacrifice of immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into the consumer's trajectory. Histories, libraries, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure.<1>p. 709</1>

The social function of property and of intellectual property prevents exclusivity from operating as a sufficient title to legitimize the unilateral deletion of these collections under the pretext of business freedom, economic convenience or strategic reorientation of the supplier.<1>p. 709</1>

The right to exploit, terminate or reorganize the activity remains, but it is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere. If termination is imposed, the constitutional order requires reconciling it, as far as technically and legally possible, with continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other suitable measures. The measures are alternatives, the passage does not say which of them fits each case, and the decision to terminate remains with the supplier. The construction thus stands as a doctrinal reading of the social function of intellectual property applied to exit from the market, and not as an express rule of law.
Exclusivity may organize the market; it cannot legitimize the administered destruction of others' enjoyment as a side effect of the very decision to leave it.<1>p. 709</1>

If the shutdown of the service is imposed, the constitutional order requires that it be reconciled, as far as technically and legally possible, with solutions of continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other measures suitable to prevent private architecture from becoming a lawful instrument of patrimonial and existential devastation of the consumer.<1>p. 709</1>
Does verifying supply not expose know-how?

The first is that of secrecy, according to which verifying the effects of supply would expose trade secrets and know-how, the English word for reserved technical knowledge. The answer comes from Barbosa. The know-how contract makes the supplier master between the parties, by contractual organization, and not by sovereignty enforceable against everyone, and the protection of the secret depends on the intention to keep it being regulated by obligations and on the confidential content being concretely delimited. Where there are effects on enjoyment, restoration or contestation, secrecy coexists with the minimum duty to make controllable what one intends to oppose to the consumer, and the supplier may protect the secret, but not use the word as fog to make what it does over enjoyment incontestable. The chapter on auditability shows the instruments that allow verification without exposing the asset.
Trade secrecy is not a license for a total black box when the problem has ceased to be only the asset and has become the impact of its use on the experience supplied.<1>p. 700</1>

The know-how contract allows the holder to structure a relationship in which they remain master of the competitive capacity, a dominion that does not derive from erga omnes sovereignty, but from contractual organization: the supplier is “the master between the parties” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 361)</2>. The protection of the secret depends on externalizing the intention to keep it confidential in legally structured relationships, which needs to be “regulated by obligations” <3>Barbosa</3><4>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 376)</4>.<5>p. 700</5>

Both in the regime of secrecy and in that of patents, legal protection only applies to certain and determined elements, requiring that the subject of the secret be concretely delimited to allow verification of the legal hypotheses of protection <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392)</2>.<3>p. 700</3>

Absolute shielding is also incompatible with the very regime of confidentiality, which requires specification of what is protected and concrete delimitation of the confidential content for legal protection to make sense. Where there are effects on enjoyment, restoration or contestation, the protection of confidentiality coexists with a minimum duty to make controllable what one intends to oppose to the consumer and to the protection system <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392-393)</2>.<3>p. 700</3>

The know-how contract and the protection of secrecy explain specific forms of organization of power between the parties, but their legitimacy depends precisely on structuring by obligations and on concrete delimitation of what one wishes to keep confidential <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 361; p. 376)</2>. This means that the supplier may protect its secret, but may not use the word “secret” as a magic fog to make everything it does over enjoyment incontestable.<3>p. 699-700</3>

The second, related, is that any minimum transparency would empty intellectual property, especially in software. It does not empty it, because the social function refuses the use of the program's protection as an absolute barrier to scrutiny of the effects of supply, and not the protection itself. The third is that of the system's necessity. For Miragem, clauses or practices that give the supplier unilateral direction so intense that it diminishes or suppresses the utility of the consumer's interests are materially abusive, and, when governance is anchored in software, the platform tends to present as a necessity of the system what, strictly speaking, is a choice in managing supply.

In the case of software, this is especially important, because it dismisses the recurring objection that any requirement of minimum transparency would amount to emptying IP itself. It does not. What the social function refuses is not the protection of the program, but the use of this protection as an absolute barrier to scrutiny of the effects of supply on the consumer's continued enjoyment.<1>p. 708</1>

Likewise, consumer protection acts to prevent private directive power from materially emptying the utility of the performance. The supplier's dominant position requires limits on the exercise of this power, and clauses or practices that give it intense unilateral direction over the course of the relationship, to the point of diminishing or suppressing the utility of the consumer's interests, are materially abusive <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 274; p. 387])</2>. This reasoning holds with special force when governance is anchored in software and in technical control of the environment, precisely because there the platform tends to present as a “necessity of the system” what, strictly speaking, is a choice in managing supply.<3>p. 701-702</3>

The fourth is that requiring functional equivalence would hinder innovation. The answer starts from the purpose of exclusivity itself. If it is protected to stimulate creation and organize the market, it is compatible with this purpose to require that relevant updates not empty the economic and existential function promised to the consumer or, when they do, come with adequate restoration. The social function does not freeze the ecosystem nor prevent the evolution of the service, and only blocks the use of mutability as an instrument of extraction and normalization of losses. The exclusive right may organize the market, but not unilaterally reorganize, without control, the functional and symbolic content of what was acquired under a promise of continuity.

If exclusivity is constitutionally protected to stimulate creation and organize the market, it is fully compatible with this purpose to require that relevant updates and reconfigurations not empty the economic and existential function promised to the consumer or, when they do, be accompanied by adequate restoration.<1>p. 708</1>
