It only blocks the use of mutability as an instrument of extraction and normalization of losses in a context of asymmetry of information and proof. The exclusive right may organize the market; it cannot unilaterally reorganize, without control, the functional and symbolic content of what was acquired and enjoyed under a promise of continuity.<1>p. 708-709</1>
How do the CDC and intellectual property coexist when examining a case?

When it comes time to operate, a specific parameter of reconciliation applies. Protected exclusivity over content, signs, code, systems or platform structures is not equivalent to unrestricted legitimation of the way it is exercised in the consumer relationship, and protection, intact on its own level, does not work as a general clause of immunization. The parameter dismisses a false alternative, between the almost sovereign intangibility of exclusivity, which turns it into unlimited power of government over enjoyment, and the reduction of intellectual property to a secondary obstacle, which impoverishes the understanding of an environment whose organization often depends, legitimately, on exclusive structures. The holder keeps its economic and technical prerogatives, including to organize the ecosystem and protect its assets, but not the possibility of invoking them to rule out, a priori, control of the way supply is carried out.
In IOC ecosystems, exclusivity explains the legal organization of the environment, but does not neutralize the limits that bear on the way it is exercised.<1>p. 737</1>

The existence of legally protected exclusivity over content, signs, code, systems, digital assets or platform structures is not equivalent to unrestricted legitimation of the way this exclusivity is exercised within the consumer relationship. The protection of intellectual property remains intact on its own level, but this does not authorize its invocation to work as a general clause of immunization against control of adequacy, transparency, loyalty, functional equivalence and protection of enjoyment.<1>p. 737</1>

This point is central because the relationship between intellectual property and continuous digital consumption tends to be contaminated by a false alternative. Either one asserts the almost sovereign intangibility of exclusivity, treating any consumer law interference as an undue threat to the economic architecture of the ecosystem, or one imagines that consumer protection would require reducing intellectual property to a secondary obstacle, devoid of its own legitimacy. Neither of these positions is adequate. The first turns exclusivity into unlimited power of government over enjoyment. The second impoverishes the understanding of the environment itself, whose organization often depends, legitimately, on exclusive structures of creation, licensing, technical control and economic exploitation.<1>p. 737</1>

The holder of exclusivity consequently keeps its economic and technical prerogatives, including to organize the ecosystem, protect its assets and preserve internal operating elements. What it does not keep is the possibility of invoking this position to rule out, a priori, control of the way supply is carried out.<1>p. 738</1>

The parameter also prevents the debate from being hijacked by a proprietary grammar, in which every controversy returns to the question of who the holder is or the abstract extent of the license. The relevant conflict, however, often lies in the way ownership is instrumentalized to govern enjoyment, redistribute risks, concentrate the power of alteration and hinder contestation. There is no absorption of intellectual property by the CDC, but coexistence disciplined by material harmonization, and the more intense and structural the exercise of exclusivity over the consumer's experience, the more subject it is to control as to its effects. In the order of examination, reconciliation comes after the qualification of the object, vulnerability, the duties of information and the criteria of verification, containment and imputation, as one of the operational closures of the regime, a subject also of the chapter on remedies.

The parameter of reconciliation also prevents the debate from being hijacked by an excessively proprietary grammar, in which every controversy ends up brought back to the question of who the holder of the asset is or what the abstract extent of the contractual license granted to the user is. The relevant conflict often does not lie in the direct violation of a dominial or authorial position, but in the way exclusive ownership is instrumentalized to govern enjoyment, redistribute risks, concentrate the power of alteration and hinder contestation.<1>p. 738</1>

What is required is coexistence disciplined by criteria of material harmonization, in which exclusivity and consumer protection are read as institutes that share the same constitutional space and, therefore, cannot be interpreted in a key of mutual annulment.<1>p. 738-739</1>

In ecosystems of governed enjoyment, this harmonization requires recognizing that the exercise of exclusivity becomes legally more intense, more structural and more impactful on the consumer's experience. Precisely for this reason, it also becomes more subject to control as to its effects.<1>p. 739</1>

One starts from the qualification of the object and of the regime of enjoyment, without which the rest of the analysis becomes disorganized. Next, semiotic vulnerability applies as a mechanism of governance of the meaning and intelligibility of the relationship. Only then do the duties of information and advertising become legible, in a dogmatically useful key, understood as structural forms of organizing expectation, choice and contestation. From this core, the standards that structure the institutional controllability of the conflict come into play. Open auditability, functional value equivalence, abusive teleology and rational distribution of the burdens of proof operate as criteria of verification, containment and imputation. Reconciliation with intellectual property and the primacy of functional restoration appear, at the end, as necessary operational closures, defining, on the one hand, the limit of private exclusivity before consumer protection and, on the other, the legally adequate form of response to the conflict.<1>p. 717</1>
Does consumer protection downgrade intellectual property?

The construction does not downgrade the legitimacy of intellectual property nor absorb it into the CDC as a sector detail. Intellectual property may explain the organization of the ecosystem and remains a legitimate element of it, and what it cannot do is immunize the way the ecosystem is exercised against duties of verifiable transparency, functional equivalence and control of abusiveness. The formulas of reconciliation keep qualifiers that the lawyer needs to preserve. The right to update and modify does not turn, by itself, into authorization to relevantly downgrade enjoyment without equivalence, restoration comes with the proviso where appropriate, shutdown only requires what is technically and legally possible, and moral rights enter as a subsidiary datum, without making the consumer the author of the experience.

Treating intellectual property as infrastructure of semiotic governance does not mean downgrading its legitimacy, nor absorbing it into the CDC as if it were a mere sector detail. It means recognizing that, in IOCs, it forms part of the supply regime and, for that reason, its exercise remains subject to criteria of reconciliation with adequacy, verifiability and restoration.<1>p. 695</1>

IP may explain the organization of the ecosystem. It cannot immunize the way this ecosystem is exercised against duties of verifiable transparency, functional equivalence and control of abusiveness.<1>p. 702</1>

Exclusivity remains a legitimate element of the organization of the ecosystem. What it does not do is immunize its mode of exercise against consumer protection, the social function and constitutional limits on private power.<1>p. 710</1>

Exclusivity is not to be confused with immunity against auditability. The right to update and modify does not turn, by itself, into authorization to relevantly downgrade enjoyment without equivalence.<1>p. 695</1>

For this reason too, Brazilian copyright protection offers, in a subsidiary way, an interesting clue against totalizing proprietary rhetoric. The author's moral rights are inalienable and unwaivable. This datum does not make the consumer's experience authorial nor transplant the authorial moral regime to the field of the IOC.<1>p. 709</1>

In platform-governed ecosystems, whoever controls logs, which are the automatic records of what the system did, histories, decision criteria, versions, interface records, alteration parameters and traces of sanctions controls, to a large extent, the conditions for the legal reconstruction of what happened. That is why proof is not an element external to the relationship, but part of the way it is governed, and structural opacity cannot be treated as a neutral datum of technology nor as an inconvenience to be borne entirely by the consumer.

Why do neither the impressionistic complaint nor formal equality of burdens solve it?

There is a possible mistake on each side. The first lies in the allegation and consists in asserting, impressionistically, that the consumer was manipulated or confused. This path does not serve, because what matters is to show that the communicational regime of supply was structured to produce a relevant asymmetry of understanding, comparison and contestation, traceable to legally controllable duties, defects and remedies.

The point is not to assert, impressionistically, that the consumer was “manipulated” or “confused”. The point is to show that the communicational regime of supply was structured so as to produce a relevant asymmetry of understanding, comparison and contestation, and that this asymmetry can be traced back to legally controllable duties, defects and remedies.<1>p. 605-606</1>

The second mistake lies in the procedure. In many conflicts, the disputed fact is born, transformed and remains within the supplier's technical infrastructure, the sanction may be automated and the essential information may be in internal systems inaccessible to the consumer. Demanding exhaustive proof from the vulnerable party, as if the conditions of production of the dispute were symmetrical, means, in practice, rewarding private control of obscurity, and formal equality of burdens may come to operate as a mechanism of material inequality.

In many conflicts concerning immaterial objects of consumption, the disputed fact is born, transformed and remains within a technical infrastructure controlled by the supplier. The relevant alteration does not manifest as an easily apprehensible public event. The sanction may be automated or partially automated. The reconfiguration of the object may occur without a sufficient public trail. The essential information may be distributed among internal systems, databases, version records and curation criteria inaccessible to the consumer. In these scenarios, demanding exhaustive proof from the vulnerable party as if the conditions of production of the dispute were symmetrical means, in practice, rewarding private control of obscurity.<1>p. 735</1>

The consequence is the admissibility of a dynamic distribution of the burden of proof whenever the relevant evidence is structurally under the supplier's technical control. It is not a matter of dramatizing exceptionalities nor of abolishing criteria of procedural rationality. It is a matter of recognizing that formal equality of burdens may operate, in these cases, as a mechanism of material inequality.<1>p. 735</1>

On the first plane, what is alleged is not the consumer's failure to read, distraction or psychological incapacity, but a communicational and architectural structure that distributes power. The platform controls language, framings, signs of equivalence, criteria of rarity, acceptance flows, update messages and forms of visibility of the object itself, and with this it administers the means by which enjoyment will be perceived and assessed. Semiotic vulnerability can, for that reason, be alleged as a legal fact.

What instruments convert the criteria into procedure?

Open auditability and functional value equivalence only become useful when they turn into concrete mechanisms of control, because without that they remain correct in the abstract and harmless in practice. The answer does not require a new microsystem nor an autonomous regulatory regime for platforms, and it is built from the combination of objective good faith, the duty of adequate information, relational cooperation, specific relief, disclosure of documents and redistribution of the burden, already admitted in the CDC and the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The law does not need to prohibit every mutation of the service, but it needs to prevent relevant mutations from reaching the consumer as a fait accompli, without a reconstructible trail or a real possibility of contestation.

In IOCs, open auditability and functional value equivalence only become legally useful when they can be converted into concrete mechanisms of controllability of supply. Without that, they remain standards that are correct in theory, but harmless in practice, especially in environments in which the platform concentrates architecture, records, criteria of alteration and means of proof.<1>p. 656</1>

The answer does not require creating a new microsystem nor importing an autonomous regulatory regime for platforms. It can be built from the combination of objective good faith, the duty of adequate information, relational cooperation, specific relief, disclosure of documents and redistribution of the burden of proof already admitted in the CDC and the CPC<1>p. 656</1>

In other words, the law does not need to prohibit every mutation of the service; it needs to prevent relevant mutations from being pushed onto the consumer as a fait accompli, without a reconstructible trail, without a minimally intelligible explanation and without a real possibility of contestation.<1>p. 657</1>

The first mechanism is qualified communication of relevant alterations. When the change may affect the core of enjoyment, good faith requires communication oriented to the essential, prioritized and made in time for the consumer to understand, react, decide and, if necessary, contest, without devices that turn the exercise of the right into a documentary via crucis or a treasure hunt. The same duty prevents fictitious acceptance, so that silence, passivity or mere permanence in the environment do not count as acceptance of relevant mutations. Marques treats the conversion of silence into acceptance as an abusive practice and requires, even when the company uses these mechanisms, ample information and a reasonable period.

The point is elementary, but it tends to be solemnly sabotaged by platform practice: if the change is important enough to affect enjoyment, it is important enough to be communicated in a way the consumer can understand without having to do digital archaeology.<1>p. 658</1>
